annotations.keyFindings: Mobilisation within 24 hours shortened mean stay by 2.3 days (95 percent CI 0.6 to 4.0) in 260 randomised patients with seven-day physiotherapy.
annotations.limitations: Excluded about 30 percent of screened patients, including those with severe dementia, hypotension or delirium.

annotations.keyFindings: A three-day crude difference in stay disappeared after adjustment for frailty, delirium and postoperative hypotension (hazard ratio for discharge 1.03).
annotations.limitations: Adjustment for postoperative conditions may remove a real effect.

annotations.keyFindings: Trials: stay shorter by 1.9 days with high heterogeneity; observational studies inconsistent; trials excluded many patients with dementia or delirium.
Delays were due to hypotension (31 percent), no weekend physiotherapist (28 percent), delirium (22 percent) and pain (12 percent).
Hypotension and delirium both delay mobilisation and predict long stays; adjust for pre-surgical characteristics and report estimates with and without postoperative conditions.
Weekend cover raised mobilisation within 24 hours from 48 to 71 percent; stay fell by 1.1 days with an interval including no change.
annotations.limitations: One unit; a discharge coordinator started in the same period.

annotations.keyFindings: Physiotherapy and nursing entries agreed within two hours for 84 percent of patients; reading one set of notes took a median of 22 minutes.
annotations.limitations: One hospital; electronic and paper notes mixed.

claims.text: In a randomised trial, physiotherapist-led mobilisation within 24 hours shortened mean length of stay by 2.3 days.
claims.passage: Mean length of stay was 13.1 days with early mobilisation and 15.4 days with usual care
claims.interpretation: Benefit in selected patients with seven-day physiotherapy; applicability to excluded patients unknown.

claims.text: In a national registry, the crude difference in stay disappeared after adjustment for frailty, delirium and postoperative hypotension.
claims.passage: the hazard ratio for discharge was 1.03 (95 percent CI 0.97 to 1.10), indicating no clear difference
claims.interpretation: Either confounding explains the crude difference or adjustment for postoperative conditions removed a real effect.

claims.text: Whether mobilisation within 24 hours shortens stays in routine care, including patients with dementia or delirium, is uncertain: the trial evidence shows shorter stays in selected patients while adjusted routine-care data show no clear difference.
claims.location: Abstracts of the trial, the registry analysis and the review
claims.interpretation: The local study must be designed to show which reading holds in this unit's patients.

claims.text: Postoperative hypotension and delirium both delay mobilisation and predict long stays, so adjustment should rest on pre-surgical characteristics with postoperative conditions in a sensitivity analysis.
claims.passage: Postoperative hypotension and delirium both delay mobilisation and predict longer stays
claims.interpretation: Fixes the adjustment strategy before reading notes.

claims.text: Time of first mobilisation can be read from physiotherapy entries, which agree with nursing entries within two hours for 84 percent of patients.
claims.passage: The two sources agreed within two hours for 84 percent of patients.
claims.interpretation: The exposure can be measured from paper notes with a written definition.

claims.text: No physiotherapist being available at the weekend accounted for 28 percent of documented delays to first mobilisation.
claims.passage: no physiotherapist available at the weekend in 28 percent
claims.interpretation: Weekend staffing is a reason for delay unrelated to how unwell the patient is, usable as a check on confounding.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level, with conflicting evidence. A randomised trial found stays 2.3 days shorter with mobilisation within 24 hours, but it excluded about 30 percent of patients, including those with severe dementia, hypotension or delirium; a national registry found a three-day crude difference that disappeared after adjustment; a review found shorter stays in trials with high heterogeneity and inconsistent observational results. The conflict is about confounding and applicability, recorded as a high-uncertainty inference (c3). Methods guidance favours adjustment for pre-surgical characteristics, with postoperative conditions as a sensitivity analysis and weekend-related delay as a check. Mobilisation time can be read reliably from physiotherapy entries.
gradeRationale: Trial evidence of benefit in selected patients conflicts with adjusted routine-care data; heterogeneity and indirectness to patients with dementia or delirium lower certainty. Low certainty that early mobilisation shortens stays in routine care.
summary: Seven retrieved records; six claims recorded, one an inference with high uncertainty over conflicting records; overall certainty low.
